entry: Small sap-sucking [[Insect|insects]] of the family Aphididae, order [[Hemiptera]]. Common names include greenfly and blackfly, though color varies widely within a species. A typical life cycle involves flightless females giving live birth to female [[Nymph (biology)|nymphs]] without males, and the nymphs may already be pregnant, an adaptation called telescoping generations. Females breed profusely, and winged females develop later in the season to colonize new plants. In temperate regions a sexual phase occurs in autumn, and the insects often overwinter as eggs. About 5,000 species have been described, around 400 of them on food and fiber crops. Aphids are among the most destructive insect pests of cultivated plants in temperate regions: they weaken plants by sucking sap, act as vectors for plant [[Virus|viruses]], and disfigure ornamentals with honeydew and sooty moulds. Insecticide resistance and feeding on leaf undersides make large-scale control difficult.

Substance that increases libido, sexual desire or sexual behavior. Aphrodisiacs range from plants, spices and foods to synthetic chemicals such as [[MDMA]] and [[Methamphetamine]]. Those with hallucinogenic properties, such as bufotenin, have psychological effects, while smooth-muscle relaxants such as yohimbine act physiologically and increase blood flow. Claimed effects may partly reflect the [[Placebo|placebo effect]], and evidence for most natural aphrodisiacs is limited. The word derives from Greek, meaning 'pertaining to [[Aphrodite]]'.

Ancient Greek goddess of love and beauty. Her main cult centers included Cythera, [[Cyprus]], Corinth and Athens. In Homer's *Iliad* she is the daughter of [[Zeus]] and Dione, while in [[Hesiod]]'s *Theogony* she is born from sea foam. In Homer's *Odyssey* she is married to [[Hephaestus]] and is caught by him in an affair with Ares. She was one of three goddesses whose feud led to the [[Trojan War]]. The Romans identified her with [[Venus (mythology)|Venus]].

Family of mostly aromatic [[Flowering plant|flowering plants]], also called Umbelliferae and known as the celery, carrot or parsley family. It is the 16th-largest family of flowering plants, with more than 3,800 species in about 446 [[Genus|genera]]. Most species are annual, biennial or perennial herbs, and their flowers are nearly always aggregated in terminal umbels. Economically important members include [[Anise|anise]], caraway, [[Carrot]], [[Celery]], [[Coriander]], [[Cumin]], dill, fennel, [[Parsley]] and parsnip. Many species are phototoxic, such as giant hogweed and parsnip, and some are deadly, such as poison hemlock and water hemlock. The seeds often contain essential oils that give anise, cumin and coriander their flavor.

Large phylum of mainly parasitic [[Alveolate|alveolates]]. Apicomplexa are unicellular, spore-forming [[Protozoa|protozoans]], and most are obligate endoparasites of animals. The exception, *Nephromyces*, is a symbiont in marine animals. The name comes from Latin *apex* (top) and *complexus* (infolds), for the set of [[Organelle|organelles]] in the infective sporozoite that allow penetration of host cells. Most members possess a non-photosynthetic [[Plastid|plastid]] called an apicoplast. Life cycles involve asexual and sexual replication, some members use two hosts, and most use gliding motility. Diseases caused by members include [[Malaria]] (*Plasmodium*), [[Toxoplasmosis]] (*Toxoplasma gondii*) and cryptosporidiosis (*Cryptosporidium parvum*). The group includes coccidia, gregarines, piroplasms and plasmodia.

1979 American epic war film directed by [[Francis Ford Coppola]]. Inspired by [[Joseph Conrad]]'s novella *Heart of Darkness*, it moves the story to the [[Vietnam War]]. Captain Willard, played by [[Martin Sheen]], travels up a river into Cambodia to assassinate Colonel Kurtz, played by [[Marlon Brando]]. Problems lengthened shooting in the Philippines to over a year, and the film premiered unfinished at the [[Cannes Film Festival]], where it was honored with the Palme d'Or. It received eight Academy Award nominations and won for Best Cinematography and Best Sound.

Revelation of cosmic mysteries or the future by a supernatural being to a human intermediary. The word comes from Greek *apokálupsis*, meaning 'revelation' or 'disclosure'. Apocalyptic literature, a genre that originated in [[Judaism]] after the Babylonian exile, persisted in [[Christianity]] and [[Islam]]. Its visions typically use symbolic imagery from the Jewish Bible, and most texts are written under pseudonyms, claiming as author a venerated figure of earlier centuries. The [[Book of Revelation]] is the only apocalypse in the [[New Testament]], and chapters 7–12 of the Book of Daniel are the sole clear case in the Jewish Bible. [[Eschatology|Apocalyptic eschatology]] applies this worldview to the end of the world, when God brings judgment. In popular use apocalypse often means a catastrophic end-times event, but scholars restrict the term to the visionary or revelatory event.

Dogbane family of [[Flowering plant|flowering plants]], including oleander and milkweeds. Its name, from the Greek for 'away-dog', reflects that some taxa were used as dog poison. Members include trees, shrubs, herbs, stem succulents and vines, native to tropical and subtropical regions with some temperate members. Most exude a milky latex when cut, and many species are poisonous, rich in [[Alkaloid|alkaloids]] and cardiac glycosides; the latter were used as arrow poisons. The former family Asclepiadaceae is now a subfamily containing 348 genera. As of 2012 the family was described as comprising some 5,100 species in five subfamilies. Vincristine and vinblastine, used in cancer treatment, come from Madagascar periwinkle, and ornamental genera include frangipani and periwinkle.

Fifth crewed mission of the [[Apollo program]] of NASA, and the first to land humans on the [[Moon]]. Launched on July 16, 1969, from [[Kennedy Space Center]] in Florida aboard a [[Saturn V]] rocket, it carried Commander [[Neil Armstrong]], Command Module Pilot Michael Collins and Lunar Module Pilot [[Buzz Aldrin|Edwin 'Buzz' Aldrin]]. Armstrong and Aldrin landed the lunar module *Eagle* in the Sea of Tranquility on July 20, while Collins remained in lunar orbit in the command module *Columbia*. Armstrong became the first human to walk on the Moon about six hours after landing, followed by Aldrin 19 minutes later. In about two and a half hours on the surface they planted an American flag, deployed scientific instruments and collected 21.5 kg (47.5 lb) of lunar material. The crew splashed down in the [[Pacific Ocean]] on July 24. Armstrong's moonwalk was broadcast live to an estimated 600 million viewers.

Olympian god of ancient Greek religion and mythology, associated with healing, prophecy, music and archery. Son of [[Zeus]] and Leto and twin brother of [[Artemis]], goddess of the hunt, Apollo is represented as the ideal of a beardless, athletic youth. As patron deity of Delphi he was an oracular god, consulted for guidance in many matters, and he was seen as the averter of evil. Medicine and healing were associated with him, and he could both deliver people from epidemics and bring [[Plague (disease)|plague]] with his arrows. As god of music he presides over songs, dance and poetry, and the [[Lyre|lyre]] is his common attribute, with the [[Muses|Muses]] as his chorus. He was patron of herdsmen and shepherds and protector of the young. From the 5th century BC he was often identified with Helios, the personification of the Sun.

United States crewed spaceflight program led by NASA, from 1961 to 1972. Conceived in 1960 during the [[Dwight D. Eisenhower|Eisenhower]] presidency, it was dedicated to President [[John F. Kennedy]]'s goal, stated in a May 25, 1961, address to Congress, of landing a man on the Moon and returning him safely before the decade was out. [[Apollo 11]] achieved the first landing in July 1969. Five more missions landed astronauts on the Moon, the last being Apollo 17 in December 1972; 12 people walked on the Moon in six spaceflights. A cabin fire during a ground test in 1967 killed the crew of Apollo 1. After an oxygen tank exploded on Apollo 13 en route to the Moon, the Lunar Module served as a 'lifeboat' for the return. The program returned 842 pounds (382 kg) of lunar rock and spurred advances in avionics, telecommunications and computers. Its [[Skylab]] space station supported three crewed missions in 1973–1974.

Ancient Greek geometer and astronomer, known for his work on [[Conic section|conic sections]]. Building on [[Euclid]] and [[Archimedes]], he brought the theory of conics to the state prior to the invention of [[Analytic geometry|analytic geometry]], and his definitions of the [[Ellipse|ellipse]], [[Parabola|parabola]] and [[Hyperbola|hyperbola]] are those in use today. His other work, including astronomy, survives mostly as fragments quoted by later authors such as Pappus of Alexandria. His hypothesis of eccentric orbits to explain the apparent motion of the planets was commonly believed until the Middle Ages and was superseded during the Renaissance. Eutocius of Ascalon places him in the time of Ptolemy III Euergetes, and the surviving autobiographical material implies he lived and wrote in Alexandria. The Apollonius crater on the [[Moon]] is named in his honor.

Systematic defense of religious doctrines through argument and discourse. The word comes from Greek *apologia*, 'speech in defense'. Some sources identify apologetics as a separate branch of [[Theology]], especially for [[Christianity]]. Early Christian writers who defended their beliefs against critics and recommended their faith to outsiders became known as early examples of Christian apologists. Charges against Christians in the Roman Empire included cannibalism and incest, and [[Paul the Apostle]], Justin Martyr and [[Irenaeus]] defended the faith against such charges. Christian apologetics combines theology, natural theology and [[Philosophy|philosophy]] to present a rational basis for belief. Apologetic texts have also defended the Baháʼí Faith and [[Buddhism]], as in *The Questions of King Milinda*. Critics argue that evidential arguments over-rely on probabilistic evidence.

Socratic dialogue by [[Plato]], a speech of legal self-defense. It presents the speech [[Socrates]] gave at his trial in 399 BC on charges of impiety and corrupting the youth of Athens. Socrates answers the charge of not believing in the gods of the city but in other, novel *daimonia*. It is one of four Socratic dialogues, with *Euthyphro*, *Phaedo* and *Crito*, through which Plato details the final days of Socrates. Scholars debate its reliability as a record of the trial, and it is compared with the parallel account of [[Xenophon]]. Although [[Aristotle]] classified it as a genre of fiction, it is still considered a useful historical source about Socrates.

Formal disaffiliation from or renunciation of a religion. The word is also used metaphorically for renouncing a [[Political party|political party]], [[Social movement|social movement]] or sports team, and in the [[Catholic Church]] for abandoning the clerical or monastic state without leaving the religion. Few former believers call themselves apostates, because of the term's negative connotation, while sociologists use it in a technical sense without pejorative meaning. Some religious groups and states punish apostates, with penalties that include shunning, excommunication, violence or execution. In [[Islam|Islamic]] jurisprudence apostasy (*riddah*) is classified as a hudud offense warranting capital punishment under classical interpretations, a penalty codified in at least ten Muslim-majority countries, though executions are infrequent. Supporters justify it as safeguarding communal integrity. Controversy centers on the tension between [[Freedom of religion|religious freedom]] as a universal [[Human rights|human right]] and claims of religious authority over belief.

Geo-cultural region in the [[Appalachian Mountains]] of eastern North America. [[West Virginia]] is the only state entirely within it. The Appalachian Regional Commission, created in 1965, defines the region as 420 counties and eight independent cities in 13 states. Early 20th-century writers often stereotyped its people as isolated and uneducated, emphasizing moonshining and clan feuding, though sociological studies have since begun to dispel these images. Despite abundant natural resources, the region has long been associated with poverty.

Mountain system of eastern [[North America]], extending roughly 2,050 miles (3,300 km) from central Alabama to Newfoundland. Its highest peak, Mount Mitchell, rises 6,684 feet (2,037 m) in the Black Mountains subrange of North Carolina, part of the [[Blue Ridge Mountains]]. Geologic formation began about 1.1 billion years ago with the [[Supercontinent|supercontinent]] Rodinia, and three orogenies beginning around 480 million years ago make the range one of the oldest surviving mountain ranges. Erosion over 240 million years lowered its peaks to the rugged forms seen today. The ridges and valleys form a barrier to east–west travel, which shaped the expansion of the United States in the colonial era. Forests range from temperate broadleaf forest in the south to boreal forest in the north. The 2,175-mile (3,500 km) Appalachian Trail runs from Mount Katahdin in [[Maine]] to Springer Mountain in [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]].

Measure of the brightness of a celestial object as observed from Earth. The scale is reverse logarithmic, so brighter objects have lower numbers, and a difference of 1.0 corresponds to a brightness ratio of about 2.512. [[Sirius]] has a magnitude of −1.46 and [[Venus]] −4.2, while the Sun is −26.832. The faintest stars visible to the naked eye on a dark night are about +6.5. Absolute magnitude instead gives the apparent magnitude an object would have at 10 parsecs.

Process in [[Law|law]] by which a higher authority reviews a case or decision at a party's request. Appeals both correct errors and clarify and interpret the law. Appellate courts have existed for thousands of years: in the first dynasty of Babylon, [[Hammurabi]] and his governors served as the highest appellate courts, and Roman law recognized a right to appeal in the Valerian and Porcian laws from 509 BC. [[Common law|Common law]] countries did not incorporate an affirmative right to appeal until the 19th century. England replaced writs of error and certiorari with appeals in civil cases in 1873 and in criminal cases in 1907. Judicial review, which determines whether a legislative act or administrative decision is defective, is a distinct process. American courts say a judgment is 'affirmed' or 'reversed', while British courts say an appeal is 'dismissed' or 'allowed'.

Finger-like, blind-ended tube connected to the cecum of the [[Large intestine]]. The appendix averages 9 cm in length and 6 mm in diameter. Because its removal causes no side effects, it was long deemed to have no specific function. In 2007 William Parker, Randy Bollinger and colleagues at [[Duke University]] proposed that it serves as a haven for beneficial gut bacteria when illness or antibiotics flush them out. Inflammation, appendicitis, is often treated by surgical removal, an appendectomy.

Round, edible fruit of the apple tree (*Malus* spp.). The orchard or domestic apple, *Malus domestica*, is the most widely grown species in its genus. The tree originated in [[Central Asia]], where its wild ancestor, *Malus sieversii*, is still found. Apples were grown in [[Eurasia]] for thousands of years before European colonists introduced them to the American continent. More than 7,500 [[Cultivar|cultivars]] are bred for cooking, eating raw and [[Cider|cider]] or juice. Seedlings differ greatly from their parents, so cultivars are propagated by clonal grafting onto rootstocks, which control the size and growth speed of the tree. Apples are significant in many [[Myth|mythologies]] and [[Religion|religions]], including Norse, Greek and Christianity in Europe. In 2010 the fruit's genome was sequenced.

Series of microcomputers made by Apple from 1977 to 1993. Designed by [[Steve Wozniak]], the original model first went on sale on June 10, 1977. It was one of the '1977 Trinity' of home computers with the Commodore PET 2001 and the TRS-80. Unlike earlier home microcomputers sold as kits, it was a finished consumer product in a plastic case. The IIe was the series' best-selling model. The 1979 release of the [[Spreadsheet|spreadsheet]] VisiCalc helped expand its use in business. Apple sold approximately six million units across the series.

American multinational technology company headquartered in Cupertino, California, in Silicon Valley. Founded in 1976 as Apple Computer Company by [[Steve Jobs]], [[Steve Wozniak]] and Ronald Wayne, it adopted its current name in 2007 as its focus expanded from computers to [[Consumer electronics|consumer electronics]]. The [[Apple II]] was among the first successful mass-produced personal microcomputers. The Macintosh, introduced in 1984, popularized graphical user interfaces navigated by a mouse. After Jobs left in 1985, Apple lost considerable market share to lower-priced PCs running Windows. Apple bought NeXT in 1997, which brought Jobs back, and under his leadership it returned to profitability with the iMac, iPod, iPhone and iPad. Jobs resigned in 2011 for health reasons. In 2018 Apple became the first publicly traded U.S. company valued at over $1 trillion. Its contractors' labor conditions and anti-competitive tactics have drawn criticism.

Computer software intended for end-user tasks, rather than for operating or programming a computer. It includes programs such as [[Word processor|word processors]], [[Web browser|web browsers]], media players and mobile apps. Its distinction from [[Operating system|system software]] is subjective, since system software manages hardware resources while application software centers on user-facing tasks. The abbreviation *app* became popular with the 2008 introduction of the iOS App Store, and later covered end-user software on any platform after the Mac App Store (2010) and Windows Store (2011). Applications may be proprietary or [[Open-source software|open-source]], and they are often bundled in suites such as [[Microsoft Office]] and [[LibreOffice]]. A killer application is one so popular that it increases demand for its host platform; [[Spreadsheet|VisiCalc]] was the first modern spreadsheet for the [[Apple II]].

Use of mathematical methods in fields such as [[Physics|physics]], engineering, medicine, biology and finance. The term also describes the specialty in which mathematicians formulate and study mathematical models of practical problems. Historically it centered on applied analysis, especially [[Differential equation|differential equations]], approximation theory and applied probability, closely linked to Newtonian physics. Practical problems have often motivated theories that later became subjects of [[Pure mathematics|pure mathematics]]. Modern applications include [[Number theory|number theory]] in [[Cryptography]], and computational science and engineering use high-performance computing to simulate phenomena. Poincaré and Arnold denied that 'applied mathematics' is a distinct field and spoke only of applications of mathematics.
